newsitem.title: USA: Procedures ready for power transfer in Clinton op.
newsitem.headline: Procedures ready for power transfer in Clinton op.

text.p: Procedures were in place on Friday to transfer presidential authority to Vice President Al Gore in the event President Bill Clinton was put to sleep temporarily for knee surgery.
Doctors used a spinal anaesthesia to numb Clinton from the waist down that would allow the president to stay awake and avoid a transfer of power.

But White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles was at Bethesda Naval Hospital with Clinton and prepared to oversee the process in the event a transfer of power was needed under the 25th amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The transfer would require Clinton to transmit a written declaration to leaders of the House of Representatives and the Senate stating that he was unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office and making Gore the acting president, until Clinton could again fulfil his duties.
The White House said later that Clinton's surgery was almost over and doctors were "very pleased" with the outcome. No complications were reported.

Then-President Ronald Reagan temporarily transferred executive authority to his vice president, George Bush, for about eight hours in 1985 when he was under general anaesthesia for colon cancer surgery. In that case the amendment itself was not invoked, however.

In May 1991 when Bush was president, he was prepared to transfer power to his vice president, Dan Quayle, when he was being treated for a heart condition called atrial fibrillation, but the transfer never became necessary.
McCurry told reporters at the hospital that the White House has an existing written plan laying out the procedures to be followed in the event the 25th amendment were to be invoked.
"We do not make that public because in fact some aspects of that are classified. It does require a written transmission of letters," McCurry said, adding that such letters had not been drafted.

"We have through counsel and through contacts with the vice president's staff made all the necessary arrangements just in case," McCurry said. "We made sure that we would be able to reach all the people that we needed to reach."
